cultivar: Mostly China-type bushes, about a quarter clonal
processing: Orthodox black tea, mostly sold through auction; the estate also makes orthodox green teas for export, including Hyson and pan-fired pellets for Morocco.
harvest_season: The peak or rush comes around April to June, after the spring rains; frost tea is made on request.
appearance_dry: Dark orthodox leaf, as is typical of Nilgiri black tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear bright amber, typical of Nilgiri black tea.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about the black tea specifically; as with other Nilgiri teas, expect a clean, fragrant, gently brisk cup.

brewing.notes: Western-style, in water just off the boil. A shorter steep suits the fragrance typical of this region.

vintage_note: The black tea mostly goes through auction, so it is seen more in blends than under its own name; retail lots are uncommon. As with other Nilgiri black tea, buy recent stock and drink it within a year or two. The green teas are export products sold separately.
description:
Craigmore is a large Nilgiri estate of about 1,200 hectares at around 5,500 feet in southern India. It stands out for an unusual mix: orthodox black tea for auction alongside green teas for export, including a sweet Hyson and pan-fired pellets made for the Moroccan market.

The bushes are mostly China-type, with about 25% clonal. About half the plucking is now mechanised, and the estate has kept tracts of shola forest and relies entirely on rainwater harvesting.

Few tasting notes exist for the black tea. Use what is typical of the Nilgiris as a guide: clean, fragrant and brisk rather than heavy, so go gently on the steep and on the milk.

You are more likely to meet Craigmore inside a blend than on a label. If you do find a named lot, the interesting comparison is its Hyson green next to the black, which shows the range one Nilgiri estate can work in.
history:
The company began as the Ceylon Land and Produce Company Limited, incorporated in 1884, the same year the estate is said to have been opened. The Inlaks Group bought it with its factories in 1977, and M.N. Bopana took over as managing director in May 2004.

Output rose from about 176,000 kg in 1990 to about 1.12 million kg in 2018-19 without new capacity, according to a trade profile.
